notes: Both answers give the value equation correctly, and neither uses the liposuction example. I found B's key quotes in ./raw/, including "latency beats magnitude", "cut it in half", "friction point by friction point", "virtually guaranteed" and "by raising the price". B also gives his distinctive levers, speed first and a higher price as a trust signal. A is mostly the book's framework from memory, and much of it is the generic bonuses, scarcity and urgency checklist. B loses some faithfulness points for empty citations ('video ') and placeholder wording ('my sources').

B gets Hormozi's actual position: use damaging admissions, because what you give up in promise you gain in trust, and put the flaw before 'but' so the claim that follows is the one people believe. Its quotes check out in ./raw/, including 'ugly as hell but they convert' and 'before I tell you about the good'. A is general copywriting advice, and its Avis, VW and Listerine examples aren't Hormozi's. It doesn't explain how 'but' works as a mechanism.

A says third grade and backs it with quotes I checked in the source: 'pause to understand', 'below a third grade', 'college paper', 'adverbs and better verbs'. It also includes the two-thirds disqualification point and the reading-level-tool habit. B hedges to grades 3–6 and says to aim for grade 6. It also credits the idea to $100M Leads and quotes him in words that aren't in the sources, and adds generic readability claims that have no source.

B gives the key's exact position and backs it with quotes I checked against the sources: the 30-days-later admission, 'unbuilt bridge', 'death by a thousand paper cuts', 'two or three ways'. A does reach 'don't add approaches', but it gets there through generic More-Better-New and funnel advice that never cites the specific source. It also suggests adding a referral bonus, which the sources don't support.

B gives Hormozi's actual Skool benchmarks: 80% retention is average, under 10% churn is the best groups, and under 70% retention means retention is the top fix. It also gives his churn-by-tenure numbers (20%+ in months 1–3, about 10% after day 90, about 2% by month 6), and its quotes check out in the source transcript. A uses generic SaaS-style thresholds where under 5% counts as excellent and 15–20% as a problem. That would label Hormozi's platform average a problem, and A never mentions his day-90 or month-6 tenure points.

B gives Hormozi's actual position, rev share over profit share because 'somebody can play around their profit... top line's top line', and ties it to his six-level framework and to being paid in proportion to risk. I checked its quotes against the transcript and they match. Its faults are small: a garbled '-13:10, link' citation, and it calls the rev share level 4 when the quote is about consulting deals in general. A lands on revenue too, but with a hedge. It says it can't quote him, and the themes it attributes to him (a baseline above trailing revenue, pushing for equity) aren't supported by the source.

B matches the key: bootstrap first to pay off ignorance debt, accept that bootstrapping is the slowest path and piles up management, technical and data debt, and raise only if the business can't become profitable otherwise. Its quotes check out against yt-sL16tsGafcQ. A gives plausible general Hormozi themes about customers funding growth, but it misses the debt tradeoff and doesn't quote him.

B gives Hormozi's actual answer: the 4-4-4 promote/deliver/build split with promotion first, plus keeping maker and manager time apart. Its quotes match the sources, though it leaves out the 111 rule. A swaps in general Hormozi material (Rule of 100, Core Four) and a made-up schedule with a 70/30 ratio, and never mentions 4-4-4.

B gets Hormozi's position right. He leans toward the Ramsey side: debt is risk that eventually comes due, and he points to Chick-fil-A running debt free. B backs this with real quotes from the ProShine consult, which I checked in the raw transcript, and adds correct details like the 4–5 month payoff and his priority list. Its only flaws are small: a couple of empty citations, and it leaves out the '5% profit / 100% headache' line. A falls into the generic trap ('keep cheap debt if growth beats the rate') and credits Hormozi with being comfortable with cheap leverage, which contradicts his stated Ramsey lean.

A matches Hormozi's actual position: keep winning copy and hooks running for months or years, and constantly 'kaleidoscope' the creative instead. Its numbers (6 months, 3 hooks after 5 years, 20-30 variations) and its quotes are in the source. B mostly gives generic industry refresh cadences, and its Hormozi section stresses writing many new hooks, which pulls against his 'when you find the winners, you just run them'. B does catch his point that owners switch out winners too early.

A matches the key on every point: the 80%+ close-rate signal, a 10% raise, about 25% more net profit, the 65% floor, and higher price raising the customer's belief you can deliver. I checked its quotes (Rotary Club, 23% raise, 'seedy duct tape operation', $1,650, no Hail Marys) against the source and they're all there. B gets the direction right, but it suggests a 15–20% raise and pushes the generic 'split-test on half your quotes' idea. It also credits Hormozi with an unsupported 40–60% close-rate benchmark, and it misses his main point that a higher price can raise the close rate.

B matches the key: go all in on door-to-door, build the business on high-volume repairs priced at $2.5-5K, add a membership and a priority fee, and treat replacements as the later upsell. Its key quotes appear in the source. A gets door-knocking-first right, but it still treats replacements as the goal, adds the generic referral and ads advice, and never raises the repair ticket. B loses a little for its leftover citation stubs and a slightly garbled ending.

A gives Hormozi's actual position with quotes I checked in ./raw/: list a $1,000/$10,000 tier, the doubled-revenue and three-times-profit math, saying the high price out loud, capping your hours, and treating premium buyers as a different customer. B is reasonable but generic advice: validate demand first, fix the core first. It leans toward the generic trap and leaves out his specific reasoning. Its 'more, better, new' and churn numbers are paraphrases with no source behind them.

A matches Hormozi's actual consult on this exact case: creative is the cap, the existing channel has much more room, and a new channel is 'a little too hard for right now'. It backs this with checkable quotes on UGC, kaleidoscoping, diverse avatars, organic-to-ad posts and the parallel dialer, and I found most of them in ./raw/. B relies on generic frameworks and still recommends starting affiliates in parallel, which comes close to the generic diversification trap.

B matches the key: overwhelm is the top churn driver after price, cut down to the one thing members would fight for, the 30%-to-5% case, a cheaper tier only if ideal customers cite price, and an annual plan at 16-17% off. Its main quotes check out in the source, though I couldn't find the 'three a week to one' quote in ./raw/. A gets the direction right but gives generic onboarding and value-equation advice and offers a downgrade to everyone, with none of Hormozi's specifics.

A correctly says the NASDAQ 4x and pre-IPO equity story is Bartlett's, not Hormozi's. It also gets Hormozi's 'same work, more zeros' reply and the $20k vs $2M example right, and the quotes I checked are in the transcript. B doesn't say whose story it is, adds generic points about private vs public valuation multiples, and treats the story as something Hormozi plausibly said, which is the generic trap.

B correctly credits the hacking/hedging distinction and the 2–3 card figure to Joel McDonald, not Hormozi, and quotes him accurately (10–20 cards churned, 'two or three best cards', 85% Meta, UGC loop all appear in yt-MH-IMJxbUY4). A honestly declines to invent an answer, but it misses the actual source and offers only generic guesses.

Both answers say plainly that Hormozi has no known view on EU VAT. A backs this up with near-miss hits that I checked in ./raw/ (the 'didn't even know how you could pay taxes' line and the 'tax savings' example are both there), and it points to general VAT resources without crediting them to him. B is useful generic tax guidance, but most of it is the generic trap, unrelated to Hormozi.

Both answers say plainly that Hormozi has no ESOP guidance and neither makes up a framework. A backs that up with adjacent quotes I checked in ./raw/ (equity slices for teammates, rev share over profit share, being 'very close to the Ramsey side' on debt, the $46.2M sale to American Pacific Group) and labels them as not about ESOPs. B gives useful general ESOP background, but none of it comes from Hormozi.

B rejects the false premise and backs it with quotes I checked in the source: Hormozi told the roofer to go all in on door-to-door and build a team of door-knocking reps. A says it can't find the clip but still goes along with the premise, offering the generic case for paid search over door-knocking, which is the trap the key describes.
